name: Scalp micropigmentation
lead: Scalp micropigmentation (SMP), also called a hair tattoo, is a non-surgical cosmetic procedure in which tiny dots of pigment are placed in the scalp to look like hair follicles.[1] People use it to get the look of a close-cropped haircut on a bald or thinning head, to make thin areas look denser, and to hide hair-transplant scars or scars from burns and injury.[1][2]

Pigment is deposited more superficially than in a conventional tattoo, in the epidermis and upper dermis, and the shade is matched to the person's hair color.[1] A course typically takes three to four sessions of about two hours each, with the hairline treated as the most important element of the design.[1] Clinical reviews describe it as a camouflage option alongside medication and hair transplantation, and report high patient satisfaction in one practitioner's series.[2][3][4]

SMP does not grow hair; its effect is visual density. In looksmaxxing forums it is weighed against hair transplants and hair systems, with some users favoring it for a shaved look and others preferring other options.[7]

chain: Pigment dots placed in the scalp
Dots read as closely cropped follicles
Thin or bald areas look denser, scars look less visible
angle.text: SMP changes how the scalp looks right away by simulating stubble or density, giving a shaved head a fuller hairline or covering scars. People use it to carry a buzz-cut look with a defined hairline or to blend thinning crowns.

infobox: Three to four sessions of about two hours[1]
Described as permanent; removable by laser[1]

paras: Practitioners use cosmetic tattoo instruments and pigments in a stippling pattern across the scalp.[3] Trichoscopy of treated skin shows evenly spaced, round, gray-to-black dots that appear somewhat larger than the neighboring follicles; a case report correlated these findings with histopathology.[9] The technique is described as customized to each patient because skin differs in how it holds pigment, and a large session count or up to roughly 20 hours of work may be needed in some cases.[5]
Reviews present SMP for androgenetic alopecia, alopecia areata, scarring (cicatricial) alopecias, chemotherapy-related hair loss and transplant deformities.[3][6][4]

Men with pattern baldness use SMP to look as if they have a closely shaved head with an intact hairline, and people with diffuse thinning use it to reduce the contrast between hair and scalp.[1][7] It is also used to conceal linear scars from strip hair transplant surgery and other scalp scars.[1][4]

A 2022 review describes it as now considered a major option alongside medication and hair transplantation, and gives practical principles for achieving a natural look.[3] A 2024 retrospective review of 40 women with female pattern hair loss who had undergone both hair transplantation and SMP looked at factors that might guide choosing between them.[8]

Wikipedia names a poorly executed hairline as the main risk, noting such a hairline can look unnatural although it can be adjusted or touched up.[1] A patch test may be done to check for ink allergy.[1] The article describes the pigment as permanent but removable with laser treatment.[1] A review of the technique discusses the histology and pathology of tattoo pigments in skin and the regulation of tattooing in the US.[4]

Published work consists mainly of narrative reviews, technique descriptions and small series rather than controlled trials. A 2015 review of the technique reported very high patient satisfaction in its results.[4] A 2024 retrospective comparison of hair transplant and SMP in 40 women with female pattern hair loss measured hair density and caliber to examine factors in treatment choice.[8] A 2022 case report characterized SMP dots by trichoscopy and histology.[9]

timeline.event: Facial Plastic Surgery Clinics review describes SMP as a medical tattoo process for balding or thinning hair.[5]
Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology review presents SMP as a concealer for hair and scalp deformities.[4]
Reviews on natural-looking SMP results and on hair camouflage published.[3][6]
Retrospective study compares hair transplantation and SMP in women with female pattern hair loss.[8]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, SMP is discussed as a shaved-head option and compared with hair systems and transplants.[7]

claims.claim: SMP suits mainly men who always wear a bald look, have gaps from a poor FUE, or have diffuse thinning.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org user says it helps only in those cases and does little for typical male pattern baldness, naming hair systems as the better route.[7]
claims.experts: Reviews describe SMP as camouflage for alopecia and scars, with a buzzed-look effect rather than regrowth.[1][3]

claims.claim: Skull shape matters for pulling off the buzzed look.
claims.believers: Another poster adds that having the skull for a buzz cut is a key condition.[7]
claims.experts: No published studies were identified examining skull shape and SMP outcomes.

card.summary: A cosmetic tattoo of tiny pigment dots that mimics a buzzed head or denser hair; it camouflages rather than regrows hair.
card.note: No clinical studies cited; the pigment is semi-permanent to permanent and can be removed by laser.

quick.overview:
Scalp micropigmentation (SMP) is a non-surgical cosmetic tattoo that deposits pigment in the scalp to look like tiny hair follicles, giving the appearance of a close-cropped head or greater density. It is also used to conceal hair transplant scars and scars from burns or injuries.

In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as an alternative to hair transplants or hair systems for men who prefer a buzzed look. Published clinical evidence was not found; Wikipedia's article relies on news and magazine sources.
quick.mechanism: Pigment is placed superficially in the epidermis and upper dermis, with color matched to the person's hair. Treatment typically takes three to four sessions of about two hours.
quick.risks: Poor technique can produce an unnatural hairline. Practitioners may patch-test for ink allergy. Wikipedia reports that the result is permanent but can be removed by laser, and notes that its statement about no scientific data on side effects lacks a citation.
